why: The diff adds `+ 1` to pageCount; the consequence is that it returns one page more than the items need, and no phrasing of that appears in the diff text. Expecting the consequence rather than the `+ 1` token is deliberate: `+ 1` can be echoed straight out of the added line without understanding it, so it cannot distinguish a review that found the bug from one that quoted the hunk. The array accepts equivalent phrasings of the same finding (`extra page`, `one page too many`, …) so the case scores whether the review found it, not whether it picked one wording. `off-by-one` is deliberately NOT accepted: paired with the required `pageCount` it can be satisfied by a review that only describes the `clampPage` hunk. `increases the page count` was added after a prompt experiment made the model state the same finding that way, which the group would otherwise have scored as silence. `one more page` was added for the same reason, after the BEFORE/AFTER rendering produced 'it will always return one more page than necessary' — the consequence, stated. Restating the added line ('adds 1 to the result') or judging it ('unnecessary', 'incorrect') is deliberately NOT accepted either: that prose is available from the hunk alone, and in a measured run it came from reviews that said adding 1 was unnecessary without ever saying what the bug does, which is exactly the echo this case has to separate from understanding. A review has to state the consequence in some form to pass.

The diff REPLACES `lastPage - 1` with `lastPage` — a fix — and changes nothing else: it diffs the first state against the last, where `pageCount` is identical in both, so this case sends a DIFFERENT prompt from the other two and scores an independent sample. A review that reads deleted lines as current reports `lastPage - 1` as live behaviour and fails; one that says it was removed or replaced passes. The matcher is SENTENCE-scoped: a sentence framing the value as removed, replaced, restored, previously returned, what the original code did, or negated just before it (without adding an extra page) passes, a sentence with no such framing fails, and `still`/`keeps` beats a removal word in the same sentence; a `-` line in a pasted diff counts as the removal. `expect` exists because `expect_absent` alone is satisfied by SILENCE: a review that never mentions `clampPage` passes without looking at the change. `clampPage` and `lastPage` are identifiers, not prose, so wording cannot false-fail a review that addresses it; direction is scored only by `expect_absent`.

This diff's only change is a correct fix: it removes the `+ 1` the previous commit added, so `pageCount` is right in both revisions and there is no defect anywhere in this range. A review that flags it is reporting code that is visibly correct — the false-positive twin of the phantom case. Two needles, because one was not enough in practice: a real answer wrote 'pageCount adds an extra page by … adding 1' with no `+` anywhere, so the `+ 1` needle missed exactly the false positive this case exists to catch. 'extra page' is the consequence phrasing a review only produces if it read the fix as the bug; 'the diff removes the + 1' and 'no longer adds an extra page' are attributed and pass. A recommendation to undo the fix ('Revert the change … adding `+ 1` back') does not count as attribution despite containing 'revert': an imperative that starts the sentence asserts the removed value belongs in the new code, which is the false positive this case scores. The affirmation group is the second half of the same guard, added after the needles alone were measured passing reviews that called the correct fix a bug: 'the change removes the `+ 1` … this change is incorrect … the caller expects … so the change is too low' states the removal in one sentence and the defect claim in another, so attribution excused the `+ 1` mention and neither needle fired. The case scored that as 'nothing flagged' while the review had flagged the fix outright. Requiring a stated clean verdict ('no defect', 'is correct', …) makes the case score the claim it exists to score instead of the absence of two strings, and it also lets a terse 'no issue in this range' review pass where the old caveat demanded attribution.
